newsitem.title: USA: NYS gov expects to meet Speaker's terms on LIPA.
newsitem.headline: NYS gov expects to meet Speaker's terms on LIPA.

text.p: The New York State Assembly Speaker said Tuesday he would approve a controversial plan to lower Long Island's electricity rates if certain conditions were met, a requirement that looked likely to be met.
Governor George Pataki wants the state to partly take over the Long Island Lighting Company saying this would cut rates on Long Island, some of the highest in the nation.

However, the plan bogged down after the Assembly held public hearings that raised a number of questions about whether it really would slash rates by 20 percent and whether the transaction depended too heavily on tax-exempt borrowing.
"We are looking at the conditions and we're hopeful that they can all be met to his satisfaction by tomorrow morning so this will go forward," Pataki told reporters in Albany.

The Public Authorities Control Board, which has to approve tax-exempt bond sales, Wednesday plans to vote on the deal. Silver, along with Pataki and the Senate Majority Leader, Joseph Bruno, holds veto power over the board's decisions.

Pataki's plan cannot go ahead unless the board approves a $7.3 billion bond sale--which would be the nation's biggest--by the Long Island Power Authority (LIPA). The Authority would use the money to buy assets from LILCO and Brooklyn Union Gas, which plan to merge.
Officials from LIPA and LILCO also predicted Assembly Speaker Sheldon Silver's requirements would be met.

However, at least one opponent of the deal showed no sign of backing down. Paul Tonko, the head of the Assembly's energy chair, in an unusual public clash, released a letter he wrote to Silver in which he recommended that Silver reject the deal. The Suffolk County legislature, whose strong opposition to LILCO's Shoreaham nuclear plant in Brookhaven helped prevent the utility from ever opening it, recently released a critical study of the deal, and plans to hold hearings about it.

Tonko, who has held hearings on the governor's plan, said technological improvments could cause customers to leave LIPA for less costly suppliers. He warned that if LIPA cannot repay the debt, Albany might have to take on the burden.

"As for Long Island's customers, today's ratepayers will receive virtually all the benefits, while future ratepayers absorb all the risk and responsibility. Mortgaging Long Island's future should not be the result of this or any other plan." Saying LILCO shareholders and its balance sheet were the biggest winners under the governor's plan, Tonko said the company would recover nearly $5 billion in potentially stranded costs. The term refers to unprofitable investments, like LILCO's shuttered Shoreham nuclear plant in Brookhaven.

The deal would settle a big property tax case LILCO won against Suffolk County over assessments on the Shoreham plant. Tonko, who accused LILCO of dictating terms, added the plan favored Long Island over upstate as LIPA would buy LILCO's 18 percent stake in the Nine Mile II nuclear plant. "Long Island ratepayers should not be forced to absorb the entire risk of owning a nuclear power plant that Pataki Administration officials described as having a "negative value."
